editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We present a new method for reducing the size of graphs with a given property. Our method, which is based on clausal proof minimization, allowed us to compute several 553-vertex unit-distance graphs with chromatic number 5, while the smallest published unit-distance graph with chromatic number 5 has 1581 vertices. The latter graph was constructed by Aubrey de Grey to show that the chromatic number of the plane is at least 5. The lack of a 4-coloring of our graphs is due to a clear pattern enforced on some vertices. Also, our graphs can be mechanically validated in a second, which suggests that the pattern is based on a reasonably short argument.

title.title: Computing small unit-distance graphs with chromatic number 5

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We present an embedding of a 61-vertex, 5-chromatic graph of girth 4 in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) as a unit-distance graph (UDG). We speculate that no 6-chromatic case exists, even though 6-chromatic UDGs in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with girth 3 exist having as few as 47 vertices. However, our discovery provides motivation to seek 5-chromatic cases with larger girth, not least because there exist 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs in the plane with arbitrary girth.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We introduce a new graph minimization method, in which it is required to preserve some graph property and there is an effective procedure for checking this property. We applied this method to minimize 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs and obtained a graph with 509 vertices and 2142 edges.

title.title: Graph minimization, focusing on the example of 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs in the plane

editorial_contributions.text:
The chromatic number of the plane (CNP) is the minimum number of colors required to color the plane in such a way that there exists no monochromatic pair of points with distance \(1\). The problem was posed around 1950 and the early work on CNP showed that the chromatic number is between \(4\) and \(7\). The lower bound is due to the Moser Spindle graph, a \(7\)-vertex unit-distance (UD) graph with \(11\) edges. In a UD graph, the vertices are points in the plane and they are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is exactly \(1\). The upper bound can be shown by a tessellation of the plane using hexagon tiles for which the maximum distance within a tile is slightly smaller than \(1\). Each tile has a single color and tiles of the same color can be placed more than distance \(1\) from each other.

\textit{A. D. N. J. de Grey} [Geombinatorics 28, No. 1, 18--31 (2018; Zbl 1404.05063)] improved the lower bound of CNP by constructing a 1581-vertex UD graph with chromatic number \(5\). Several interestig results followed but existing techniques appear insufficient to construct unit-distance graphs with chromatic number \(6\), if they exists. Important insights might come from odd-distance (OD) graphs, in which two points are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is odd. To encourage research in this direction, the authors pose the challenge of constructing an odd-distance graph of chromatic number \(6\) or proving that it doesn't exist. Furthermore, a \(5\)-chromatic unit-distance graph of 1441 vertices without Moser Spindles is presented.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The chromatic number of the plane problem asks for the minimum number of colors so that each point of the plane can be assigned a single color with the property that no two points unit-distance apart are identically colored. It is now known that the answer is \(5,6\), or 7. Here we consider the problem in the context of the hyperbolic plane. We prove that there exists a distance \(d\approx 1.375033509\) so that every 4-coloring of the hyperbolic plane contains two points distance \(d\) apart, which are identically colored.

title.title: A 5-chromatic same-distance graph in the hyperbolic plane

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: With regard to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem, several 5-chromatic unit distance graphs in the Euclidean plane have been discovered in recent years. While most constructions rely heavily on the Moser spindle, a few recent examples completely avoid it, the smallest one consisting of 1441 vertices. In this note, we introduce an original geometric approach to constructing such graphs by utilizing the arcs of a 7-fold symmetric unit distance graph on 21 vertices, and obtain a Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices. While this is not a record small result, it arises from a straightforward, structured rule rather than a purely automated or brute-force search.

editorial_contributions.text:
This interesting survey paper describes the origin of the three color problem and virtually all the major results and conjectures existing in the literature. Its chapters are the following: 1. Introduction. 2. The origin of the three color problem (Heawood's second paper, the three color theorem). 3. Basic results (three interrelated results, outerplanar and cubic graphs, Brook's theorem (cubic case)). 4. Triangle-free graphs and chromatic number. 5. Grötzsch's theorem (variations on Grötzsch's approach). 6. Grünbaum's theorem and Aksionov's theorem. 7. The distance of the triangles. 8. Uniquely 3-colorable planar graphs. 9. Restricting 4-cycles and 5-cycles. 10. Algorithms and complexity (the Petford-Welsh algorithm). 11. Geometric problems (plane 4-regular graphs with cycle-decompositions, the circle-triangle conjecture). 12. Relationship to four coloring (triangle-colored graphs, Toft's color reduction). 13. Counting 3-colorings. 14. Applications of 3-coloring (Chvátal's art gallery theorem, computing with 3-colorable graphs). 15. Nowhere-zero 3-flows. 16. Conclusions. The bibliography includes 128 references and an appendix contains an outline of a proof of Grünbaum's theorem.

title.title: The state of the three color problem

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: A \(t\)-tone coloring of a graph assigns \(t\) distinct colors to each vertex with vertices at distance \(d\) having fewer than \(d\) colors in common. The \(t\)-tone chromatic number of a graph is the smallest number of colors used in all \(t\)-tone colorings of that graph.

 We discuss bounds for this number, and we exactly determine the value for several of classes of graphs, including cycles and trees. Cubic graphs with 2-tone chromatic number 5 are shown to be equivalent to graph covers of the Petersen graph. Properties of Petersen covers are analyzed.

title.title: Constructing 5-chromatic unit distance graphs embedded in the Euclidean plane and two-dimensional spheres

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0548.00012.] 


In his well-known book ``Untersuchungen zum Vierfarbenproblem'' (1969; Zbl 0187.209)], the author defined the important concepts D-reduciblity and C-reducibility used in the proof of the four colour theorem by \textit{K. Appel} and \textit{W. Haken} [Ill. J. Math. 21, 491-567 (1977; Zbl 0387.05010)]. In the present paper a new type E-reducibility is defined and explained. It is noted that for D-irreducible figures the concepts C- reducible and E-reducible are independent. The usefulness of E- reducibility for the four colour theorem is not discussed in detail, but it is noted that no planar critical 5-chromatic graph can contain an E- reducible figure. 


[Some definitions: A figure F is a connected plane graph consisting of a cycle \(C_ n\) of length n and a non-empty set of edges and vertices drawn in one side of \(C_ n\). Let \(\Phi\) (F) denote the set of all restrictions of 4-colourings of F to \(C_ n\), and let \(\Gamma\) (F) denote all the 4-colourings c of \(C_ n\) such that if c is extendable to a 4-colouring c' of a figure F' with \(C_ n\) as boundary then c' can always be changed by Kempe-chain interchanges to a 4-colouring with a restriction to \(C_ n\) from \(\Phi\) (G). If \(\Gamma\) (F) is the set of all 4-colourings of \(C_ n\), then F is said to be D-reducible. If F is D-irreducible, but contains a subfigure G with boundary different from the boundary of F, such that \(\Gamma (F)=\Gamma (F\) with the interior of G deleted), then F is said to be E-reducible].
